exercise.title: Why must other indeterminate forms be rewritten as quotients?

statement.p: Forms such as 0\cdot\infty, \infty-\infty, 0^0, and 1^\infty are also indeterminate. In your own words, why does l’Hospital’s Rule not apply to them directly, and what is the point of algebraically turning them into a 0/0 or \infty/\infty quotient first?

hint.p: The rule is a statement about quotients whose numerator and denominator both vanish or both blow up. Other forms need a rewrite before that hypothesis is even available.

paragraphs.title: Derivative quotient has no limit
paragraphs.p: Sometimes l’Hospital’s Rule gives no conclusion, even though the original limit exists.
But the quotient of derivatives is
which has no limit as x\to\infty.

There is no contradiction. l’Hospital’s Rule says that if the derivative quotient has a limit, then the original quotient has that same limit. It does not say that the derivative quotient must have a limit whenever the original quotient does.

exercise.title: When can l’Hospital’s Rule not be used, or give no conclusion?

statement.p: Differentiating a quotient that is not indeterminate can produce the wrong limit. Even for an indeterminate quotient, the derivative ratio may fail to have a limit while the original quotient still does. In your own words, why is the rule a one-way implication, and what must we check before using it?

hint.p: First check the form. Then remember: if the derivative quotient has a limit, the original does too. The converse is not promised.

subsection.title: Where this points
subsection.p: l’Hospital’s Rule turns some hard limits into derivative limits. It works because, near a point, differentiable functions are controlled by their local linear parts.

But every theorem in this chapter has boundaries. Fermat’s theorem needs an interior point and differentiability. The Mean Value Theorem needs continuity and differentiability. The second derivative test can be silent. l’Hospital’s Rule needs an indeterminate form and a derivative quotient that settles.
The next warning examples collect those boundaries, because knowing when a theorem cannot be used is part of knowing the theorem.
